# English

## What an AI agent can and cannot do for a Malaysian SME

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-an-ai-agent-can-do
Checked: 2026-11-23

An AI agent runs a loop by itself: it reads a task, calls tools, looks at the result and decides the next step until the job is done. That covers repetitive work with a clear finish line. It does not cover judgement, money it is not authorised to move, or anything a customer would need explained to them by a person.

## What is an agent, as opposed to a chatbot?

An agent acts between steps; a chatbot only answers. The difference is that an agent has tools it can call, a loop that continues after a tool returns, and a transcript of what it did.

Anthropic's own wording for the layer that runs this is an agent harness that "runs the agent loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure" ([Claude Code docs, read 23 Nov 2026](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview)). Two consequences follow for a small business: the agent can touch real systems, and the harness, not the model, decides what it is allowed to touch.

## What can it do unattended?

![Three panels: work that runs unattended such as sorting an inbox; work the agent prepares for a human to approve such as refunds and customer messages; work that is not for an agent such as judgement calls and physical tasks](/figures/what-an-ai-agent-can-do.svg)
*Sort the work before you choose a tool: unattended, prepared, and not agent work.*

Unattended work is work where a wrong answer is cheap to spot and cheap to undo.

| What it does on its own | Why it qualifies |
| --- | --- |
| Read an inbox and sort messages into buckets | A misfiled email is visible and reversible |
| Extract fields from an invoice or delivery order and enter them | The source document stays available for comparison |
| Copy data between two systems on a schedule | A failed copy can be re-run |
| Draft replies, reports or summaries for someone to send | A person still presses send |
| Watch a queue and alert a human when a threshold trips | The agent escalates rather than acts |

## What needs a human before it happens?

Approval work is work where the cost of a wrong action is not recoverable by re-running it.

| Needs a human | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Anything that moves money: refunds, payments, waivers | A wrong transfer is not undone by an apology |
| Sending a message to a customer on your behalf | Tone and commitment are business decisions |
| Deleting or overwriting a record | There is nothing to restore from |
| Changing prices, stock levels or availability | A wrong price is honoured, not corrected |
| Anything legal or regulatory: e-Invoice submissions, contracts, filings | The liability sits with the business, not the agent |

The practical shape is: let the agent prepare, and let a person approve. An agent that drafts a refund and waits for a click saves the typing without taking the risk.

## What can it not do at all?

Four categories, and no amount of prompting changes them.

1. **Judgement calls with no rule to follow.** Whether a complaint is fair, whether a supplier is trustworthy, whether to keep a client. An agent can gather the facts; the decision is not a fact.
2. **Anything physical.** Deliveries, installations, inspections. A WhatsApp bot can book a technician; it cannot change a part.
3. **Knowledge it does not have.** An agent answers from what it can reach. If your stock is in someone's head, the agent will be confidently wrong.
4. **Guaranteed accuracy.** Every agent produces a plausible wrong answer sometimes. That is why the approval column exists.

## What does it cost in ringgit?

Two bills, and the smaller one is the one people worry about.

**Running it.** Token rates are published, so this is arithmetic rather than a guess. At 2,000 input and 500 output tokens per task, Claude Haiku 5.5 costs `0.002 million × USD 0.10 = USD 0.0002` for input plus `0.0005 million × USD 0.50 = USD 0.00025` for output, which is USD 0.00045 a task. At the Bank Negara middle rate of **4.1145** (read 19 November 2026), that is about RM0.00185. A thousand tasks a month is **RM1.85**.

**Building it.** Malaysian publishers quote project prices for automation work: **RM400** for a simple process build ([Pang Jun Han, read 23 Nov 2026](https://pangjunhan.vercel.app/ai-automation)) and **RM6,000-plus** for autonomous task execution ([Autoflow Solutions, read 23 Nov 2026](https://www.autoflow-solutions.com/my/services)). A starter workflow build from a studio starts at **RM1,500** ([KodeSME, read 23 Nov 2026](https://kodesme.klyihao.com/)).

So the build is hundreds to thousands of ringgit and the running cost is a few ringgit. Anyone quoting you a large monthly token bill for a small business workflow is either wrong or selling something else. What the rate cards do not state is the monthly support fee after launch, so ask for it before you compare quotes.

## How do I tell a demo from something that keeps running?

A demo works once, in front of you. Something that keeps running survives a bad day. Six checks, and the answers are things, not adjectives.

1. **Show me the transcript.** A working agent records what it did, step by step. If there is no log, there is no evidence it ran.
2. **What happens when a step fails?** Retry, queue or alert. Silence is not an answer.
3. **What is it allowed to touch?** The list of systems, read or write, should be short enough to say aloud.
4. **Who owns the keys and the accounts?** Yours, in your account, revocable.
5. **What happens when the vendor changes something?** Ask who fixes it and at what price.
6. **Who is watching it next month?** An agent with no owner stops being maintained the week after the invoice is paid.

## FAQ

### Is an AI agent the same as automation software?

No. Classic automation follows rules you wrote, exactly, in order. An agent decides the next step itself within the tools and permissions it has, which is why the permissions column matters more than the model choice.

### Do I need a developer to run one?

To build the integrations, usually yes: an agent is only as useful as the systems it can reach. To operate one, no, if the work is approval-based: a staff member reviewing the queue is the human in the loop.

### Can an agent file my e-Invoice submissions?

It can prepare them, and it should not submit them unreviewed. The liability for a wrong submission is the business's, not the tool's, so the accountable person signs off until you have months of clean runs.

### What is the first thing worth automating?

The task your team does most often that has a clear finish line and a cheap mistake: invoice entry, order copying, or triaging an inbox. Start where a wrong result is visible the same afternoon.

## What e-Invoice automation covers, and what stays with a person

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-einvoice-automation-covers
Checked: 2026-11-23

Every taxpayer band is now in force, including the band between RM3 million and RM5 million, which sits inside phase 4 and outside the exemption. Automation can create, validate and submit the document and handle the 72-hour correction window. It cannot decide whether a transaction is unusual, and it cannot carry the legal liability for a wrong one.

## Who has to file, and since when?

The bands below are LHDN's own, from a timeline page that states its update date as 30 August 2026.

| Phase | Annual income or sales | Started | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | more than RM100 million | 1 August 2024 | In force |
| 2 | more than RM25 million up to RM100 million | 1 January 2025 | In force |
| 3 | more than RM5 million up to RM25 million | 1 July 2025 | In force |
| 4 | up to RM5 million | 1 January 2026 | In force |
| Exemption | less than RM3 million | — | Exempt as printed |

The gap worth reading twice is between RM3 million and RM5 million. The exemption covers less than RM3 million, and phase 4 covers up to RM5 million, so a business turning over RM4 million is in scope. That is not an interpretation: it is what the two lines on the same page say together.

## What is actually submitted?

![Four steps the machine performs: build the document from your records, check the TIN, pass eight validators, submit to MyInvois. Below, two outcomes: within 72 hours a buyer may reject or a seller cancel and reissue; after 72 hours cancellation is closed and a correction needs a credit, debit or refund note](/figures/what-einvoice-automation-covers.svg)
*Four steps run every submission. What happens after a mistake depends on the clock.*

An e-Invoice is the digital representation of a transaction between seller and buyer, covering business-to-business, business-to-consumer and business-to-government, and it goes to LHDN through the MyInvois system.

Four document types are named in the guideline: invoice, credit note, debit note and refund note. Two routes exist. The MyInvois Portal is manual entry by the taxpayer. The API route is documented for taxpayer ERP systems, in LHDN's own words, to "integrate with MyInvois System to automate the document processing" ([MyInvois SDK, read 23 Nov 2026](https://sdk.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/)). Authentication is separate for taxpayer systems and for intermediary systems acting on a taxpayer's behalf, and there is a TIN validation step available before submission.

## What can be automated?

Eight validators run on every submission, and they are the reason a machine does this better than a person retyping: structure, core fields, signature, taxpayer validity, referenced documents, codes, duplicates and currency.

| Task | Automated? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Building the document from your sales or purchase record | Yes | The data already exists in your system |
| Checking the TIN before submission | Yes | It is an API call, not a judgement |
| Passing the eight validators | Yes | They are deterministic rules |
| Submitting and storing the LHDN response | Yes | A receipt to keep, not a decision |
| Flagging a failed validation with the rule that failed | Yes | The rule name is in the response |
| Deciding whether a transaction is fake or genuinely unusual | No | A judgement, and one a human is liable for |
| Choosing consolidated invoicing under the relaxation | No | A policy decision with tax consequences |
| Approving a correction after 72 hours | No | Needs a reason a person can defend |

## What does the 72-hour window change?

It changes who fixes a mistake, and when. A buyer may request rejection within 72 hours of validation, and a seller may cancel within the same window. After 72 hours, cancellation is not allowed, and a correction requires a new e-Invoice in the form of a credit, debit or refund note.

That has a practical consequence for automation design: the tool should watch the clock, not just the submission. An integration that only posts documents and forgets them will leave corrections to whoever notices, which is how businesses end up issuing a note months late.

## What happens if you get it wrong?

The guidelines cite Section 120 of the Income Tax Act 1967, and they do not print a penalty figure on any page that could be read. That is a gap, not a small detail: this article will not quote a ringgit penalty, because no published amount was found.

Two dated mechanisms do soften the exposure. An interim relaxation period applies per phase, during which taxpayers may issue consolidated e-Invoices for all activities and consolidated self-billed e-Invoices without a document per transaction, and LHDN states it will not prosecute under Section 120 during that period provided the conditions are met. Separately, the voluntary disclosure programme runs from **7 July 2026 to 31 December 2027** for taxpayers who missed their mandatory start date, using document versions PKPS 1.2 or 1.3, and covers reviews and enforcement unless the disclosure breaches requirements or involves fraud, wilful default or negligence.

## What could we not verify?

The MyInvois Portal itself could not be read: a connection timeout, then only the page title, because it is a client-side application. LHDN's FAQ answers are loaded by script and were not present in the served HTML. The per-phase dates inside the relaxation table appear to be a graphic in the PDF and were not extracted. And the general guideline read was version 4.8; a newer general version may exist and was not confirmed.

## FAQ

### I turn over RM4 million a year. Am I exempt?

No. The exemption is below RM3 million, and phase 4 covers up to RM5 million, so RM4 million is in scope and has been since 1 January 2026.

### Can my accountant's system file it for me?

The submission route supports intermediaries: LHDN documents separate authentication for systems acting on a taxpayer's behalf. Liability stays with the taxpayer, so the question is who reviews failures, not who presses submit.

### Does automation remove the need for a person?

It removes the typing, the TIN check and the validator round trips. It does not remove the person who decides whether a transaction is genuine, or who signs off a correction after the 72-hour window closes.

### What happens to invoices I issued before my phase started?

The published mechanism for a missed start is the voluntary disclosure programme, running 7 July 2026 to 31 December 2027. Whether your case qualifies is a question for LHDN or your tax agent, not for this article.

### Sources

- LHDN, e-Invoice implementation timeline (updated 30 August 2026) — https://www.hasil.gov.my/e-invois/pelaksanaan-e-invois-di-malaysia/garis-masa-pelaksanaan-e-invois/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- MyInvois SDK, developer documentation — https://sdk.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- MyInvois SDK, document validation rules — https://sdk.myinvois.hasil.gov.my/document-validation-rules/ (checked 2026-11-23)
- LHDN, Garis Panduan Spesifik e-Invois Versi 4.8 (penalties, relaxation, PKPS) — https://www.hasil.gov.my/e-invois/ (checked 2026-11-23)

## Agent harness, AI harness, agent framework: what the words mean

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/agent-harness-vs-ai-harness
Checked: 2026-11-19

An agent harness is the runtime that runs a model's agent loop: it holds the system prompt, executes tool calls, manages context, applies permissions and supplies a working environment. Vendors use "agent harness" or just "harness". "AI harness" is not a phrase the official sources I opened use, and "agent framework" is a different thing again.

## Who actually says "harness"?

Anthropic says "hosted agent harness", and the DeepSeek Harness package uses the bare word as its product noun.

Anthropic's own definition is the clearest: a hosted agent harness "runs the agent loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed cloud sandbox or a self-hosted sandbox on your own infrastructure" ([Claude Code docs, read 19 Nov 2026](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview)). The installed DeepSeek Harness package uses the word the same way, as in "Harness home" for its config directory ([package README, read 19 Nov 2026](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh)). Neither treats it as a metaphor.

## What does the term imply, in practice?

Four things, and each one is a line rather than a walkthrough.

1. **Tool execution.** The harness runs the tool, not the model. The model chooses a tool and arguments, and the harness performs the call.
2. **A turn and step loop.** One message becomes a turn; the turn contains steps; each step is another exchange with the model when a tool result needs to go back.
3. **A transcript on disk.** The conversation is written to a file you can read: in this harness, compressed JSON Lines under `.dsh/sessions`.
4. **Permissions and approvals.** A harness decides what a tool is allowed to do, and records the policy. Without that, it is a chat client with extra steps.

How it walks through one message, step by step, is covered in [what an agent harness does with your request](https://upahje.my/en/articles/using-the-harness). This article is about the vocabulary, not the loop.

## Where does "AI harness" come from?

Not from the vendors I could read. Across the four official sources opened for this article, the phrase "AI harness" does not appear.

The method has a limit and I will state it: a search-engine query for the exact phrase returned a bot-check page instead of results, so I cannot claim no page anywhere uses it. What I can say is narrower and still useful: Anthropic says "agent harness", DeepSeek Harness says "harness", and neither uses "AI harness" on the pages I opened. When a blog uses "AI harness", it is borrowing the vendor word and adding a modifier that the vendors do not use.

| Term | Who uses it | What it means in that context |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Harness | DeepSeek Harness, Anthropic | The runtime that runs the agent loop and owns the environment |
| Agent harness | Anthropic, most vendor docs | The same runtime with the agent parts named: sessions, subagents, tool routing, approvals |
| AI harness | Marketing pages and blogs | No fixed meaning; on the sources read here, not a vendor term at all |
| Agent framework | Library authors | A code library for building agents, not a runtime that runs one |
| Agent workspace | OpenBot, MausBot | The product's own word for a harness plus a desktop or a machine per bot |

## Why does the distinction matter when buying?

Because the words describe what the product does to your machine and your data, and a framework is not that.

A framework is something a developer imports; it does not give you a running environment, a transcript you can read, or an approval gate. A harness does, and that is why the questions you ask a vendor differ: where does the transcript live, what may the tools touch, and who approves an action. If a product calls itself an "AI harness" and cannot answer those three, the label is decoration.

**Read next**

[What an agent harness does with your request](https://upahje.my/en/articles/using-the-harness)

[More on agent harnesses](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/definitions)

## FAQ

### Is Claude Code a harness or an app?

Both. Anthropic sells an app, and its Agent SDK documentation describes the underlying hosted agent harness that runs the loop. The word describes the layer, not the product.

### Is an agent framework the same as a harness?

No. A framework is a library you build with; a harness is the thing that runs the loop, executes tools and keeps the transcript. You can build a harness on a framework, and most products do.

### Does the word "harness" tell me whether it is open source?

No. The word describes a function, not a licence. A harness can be proprietary and cloud-hosted, or open source and local, and the label reads the same either way.

### Sources

- Claude Code docs, Agent SDK overview (hosted agent harness) — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview (checked 2026-11-19)
- DeepSeek Harness package README, installed on this machine (Harness home) — https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh (checked 2026-11-19)
- OpenBot repository and site — https://openbot.run/ (checked 2026-11-19)
- MausBot site — https://mausbot.com/ (checked 2026-11-19)

## Agent harnesses ranked: four CLIs installed on one machine

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/agent-harnesses-ranked
Checked: 2026-11-19

DeepSeek Harness scores highest at 4.35 out of 5, OpenCode second at 4.15, Claude Code third at 3.70 and Codex CLI fourth at 3.45. The scores come from five weighted criteria, each scored only from observations made on this machine on 19 November 2026. Nothing below is general knowledge about these tools.

## How were the scores built?

Each tool was scored 1 to 5 on five criteria, and the criteria were weighted for a Malaysian SME that wants automation and cost control.

| Criterion | Weight | Why it carries that weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider and cost control | 30% | The largest lever on a monthly bill is which model and which billing route you can use |
| Non-interactive automation | 20% | If it cannot run unattended, it cannot run on a schedule |
| MCP and tool integration | 20% | This decides whether the agent can touch your systems at all |
| Extensibility | 15% | Getting more behaviour without waiting for the vendor |
| Operational footprint | 15% | Disk, backups and machine cost for a small team |

A cell scores 5 only when the observation is explicit and complete. A criterion with nothing in our notes scores "not verified" and contributes nothing, rather than averaging to a polite middle. Provider and cost control, MCP and extensibility are editorial scores anchored to the line each tool has in the table, not measured quantities: the table says a tool supports a route, not how well it does it.

## What did we measure?

Four harnesses, one machine, one day. Version, install route, config, automation surface, MCP, provider choice, extensibility and disk footprint.

What that does and does not cover: all four were installed and configured on this machine, and every cell above was read from that installation by running `--version`, `--help` or inspecting the config path. I ran DeepSeek Harness end to end myself in this session. Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode were measured by Chief on the same machine the same day, and I did not use those three end to end. So this is a ranking of what we could inspect, not a claim that all four were driven through the same task.

| | DeepSeek Harness | Claude Code | Codex CLI | OpenCode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Version | 0.2.2-rc.1 | 2.1.296 | 0.146.0 | 1.18.11 |
| Install | `@deepseek-ai/dsh` npm package, booted by profile | binary at `~/.hermes/node/bin/claude` | binary at `~/.hermes/node/bin/codex` | `~/.opencode/bin/opencode` |
| Config | YAML patch layers under `$DSH_HOME/profiles` plus `cordis.patch.yml` | `~/.claude.json` plus `~/.claude/{skills,sessions,projects}` | `~/.codex/config.toml` plus `auth.json` | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` plus `opencode providers` |
| Non-interactive | profiles, including a shipped `headless` one | `-p` / `--print` | `codex exec` | `opencode run` |
| MCP | servers per profile; three were live in our session | `--mcp-config` | `codex mcp`, also `codex mcp-server` | `opencode mcp` |
| Provider choice | any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic route defined in the profile | Anthropic models, `--model` | OpenAI auth via `login`, model settings in `config.toml` | `opencode providers` manages credentials |
| Extensibility | plugin bundles, profile composition, skills, agent teams | `~/.claude/skills`, `--agents` JSON, subagents | `config.toml`, MCP, experimental `exec-server` | `opencode agent`, MCP, ACP server |
| Local footprint | 3.2 GB | 116 KB | 246 MB | 62 MB |

## What are the scores?

The ranking comes out of the arithmetic below, and the arithmetic is reproducible from the table above.

| Criterion (weight) | DeepSeek Harness | Claude Code | Codex CLI | OpenCode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Provider and cost control (30%) | 5 | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| Non-interactive automation (20%) | 4 | 4 | 4 | 4 |
| MCP and tool integration (20%) | 5 | 4 | 5 | 4 |
| Extensibility (15%) | 5 | 5 | 3 | 4 |
| Operational footprint (15%) | 2 | 5 | 4 | 5 |
| Weighted total | 4.35 | 3.70 | 3.45 | 4.15 |

Footprint was scored on a stated scale: 5 for under 100 MB, 4 for under 500 MB, 2 for under 5 GB. Non-interactive automation scores 4 rather than 5 for all four because each has one documented route and we did not test a scheduled run for any of them.

## What does each tool win on?

DeepSeek Harness wins on provider choice, MCP and extensibility, and loses on disk.

Its provider line is the only one that reads "any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic route", which is the 30% criterion doing most of the work. Its MCP is per-profile with three servers live during our session. Extensibility covers plugin bundles, profile composition, skills and agent teams. Against that, 3.2 GB is about 13.3 times Codex and roughly 28,900 times Claude Code on disk, which is why it takes a 2 on footprint.

OpenCode is the most even tool in the set: 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, with no single weak cell.

It has no 5 outside footprint, and no 3 or lower anywhere. For a small team that would rather not have a surprise, that shape is the argument.

Claude Code wins on footprint and extensibility and is restricted on provider.

At 116 KB it is the smallest install of the four, about 550 times smaller than OpenCode's 62 MB, and its skills plus subagents are the most complete extensibility story we observed. The provider line, "Anthropic models, `--model`", is what holds it to 3.70 despite that.

Codex CLI wins on MCP, because it is the only one of the four documented here as both an MCP client and an MCP server.

Its automation route (`codex exec`) is solid and its footprint is mid-pack. The provider line is OpenAI-only through `login`, and `exec-server` is marked experimental, which is what puts it fourth.

## What did we not verify?

OpenMausBot is out, and not because it lost. The binary is present but errors on launch, its global install and data directory are gone, and its systemd unit is inactive. We tested it and it could not run, so it is not scored and it is not ranked last.

Not verified for any of the four: response quality, latency, token cost, reliability over a week, or behaviour under load. We measured what is in the table and nothing else. A version bump can change any cell here, which is the risk in publishing version-pinned numbers: 0.146.0 and 1.18.11 are today's values, not permanent properties.

## How can I re-run this check?

Four commands and a filesystem check, and you can audit every number in the tables.

1. Run `--version` on each binary to get the four version strings.
2. Run `--help` on each to see the non-interactive flags and MCP subcommands listed above.
3. Read the config paths in the table: `$DSH_HOME/profiles`, `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex/config.toml`, `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`.
4. Run `du -sh` on `~/.dsh`, `~/.claude`, `~/.codex` and `~/.config/opencode` for the footprints.

## FAQ

### Does the ranking change if I care about cost more than 30%?

Yes, and the table lets you recompute it. Raising provider and cost control to 40% and dropping footprint to 5% keeps DeepSeek Harness first and widens its lead over OpenCode, because the gap between them sits almost entirely in that criterion. Recomputed on the same cells, that weighting gives DeepSeek Harness 4.65 and OpenCode 4.05.

### Why rank at all if the numbers are version-pinned?

Because a buyer still has to choose this week, and a stated method with a re-run recipe is checkable. The alternative, an unranked list with no weights, hides the same judgement behind prose where nobody can audit it.

## What automation work costs in Malaysia: published rates, six sources

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/automation-rates-malaysia-published
Checked: 2026-11-19

Published prices for automation work in Malaysia run from RM400 for a simple process build to RM6,000-plus for autonomous task execution. Those figures and 28 more below come from six Malaysian publishers, with the publisher, unit and date on every row. Four are studios, one is an independent practitioner, and one is a freelance profile; the only per-hour figure comes from that profile. Solo freelancers usually quote per job rather than publish, so this table is published supply, not the whole market.

## Who publishes these numbers, and who does not?

The figures below come from pricing pages of Malaysian automation providers and from one Malaysian freelance profile. Every row carries the date it was read: 19 November 2026 for the studio and platform pages, and 27 October 2026 for the independent practitioner's page.

What could not be read matters as much. The global marketplaces are unmeasured here: Upwork returns HTTP 403 with a Cloudflare block, Fiverr returns a bot challenge, Jobstreet returns a Cloudflare interstitial, and Indeed and Maukerja render their listings only in JavaScript. Not one Upwork or Fiverr profile rate could be collected, so nothing here should be read as what a globally-priced freelancer charges. These bands describe the local published-supply layer: agencies with a price list, and one marketplace profile with an hourly rate.

Two further exclusions. Every "quote on request" tier is excluded, because a quote is not a rate. Freelancer.com profiles that price in USD are excluded, even where the person is Malaysian, because the number is not a Malaysian price.

## What does a published automation build cost?

## What does an integration cost?

No Malaysian publisher in this set states a per-integration price, so no per-integration market rate is claimed here. What is published is subscription tiers that include connectors and API integration.

That is a real limit, not a formatting choice. The one build price that names integration work as part of the deliverable is a 3 to 5 workflow project from RM4,000. KodeSME's custom tier advertises integrations with existing systems and prices them as "Quote". BlueAura describes a one-time implementation fee without a number. A buyer asking "what does one API integration cost in Malaysia" will not get an answer from published pages, and this article will not invent one.

## Why do the same tasks carry different units?

Because the publishers are selling different things: a session of someone's time, a project with a defined end, or an ongoing subscription.

RM400 per 4-hour session and RM1,500 per project are not competing prices. The first is labour, and you can buy two sessions and still have no working system. The second assumes a defined scope. The third, a monthly retainer, buys attention rather than delivery. Comparing them without converting to what you actually get is the most common way a buyer misreads a table like this.

The dates matter for the same reason. Several pages carry no publication date, so the row date is the day the price was read, not the day it was published. A price read on 19 November 2026 may have been written in 2025 and not updated.

## What changes the price of a quote?

Six things, and each one appears in the table above as a different tier rather than a discount.

1. How many systems are connected. Every publisher prices by process or workflow count, not by hours.
2. Whether approvals are involved. KodeSME's growth tier adds approval flows and a dashboard at a higher price than the starter tier.
3. Whether a human reviews the output. Document extraction with a review step is priced per thousand pages by BlueAura.
4. Whether the work is monitored after launch. Every publisher here has a monthly tier; some call it a care plan, some a retainer.
5. Whether the build touches existing accounting or project software. That is the top of Pang Jun Han's range, RM1,600 to RM4,000.
6. Whether you buy a session or a scope. The only per-hour figure in the set belongs to a freelance profile, not to any of the studios.

## How do I compare two quotes when the units differ?

Convert both to the same three numbers before you compare: total cost to a working system, monthly cost after launch, and what each one excludes.

A RM400 session and a RM1,500 project both look small next to a RM6,000 build, and none of them is comparable until you ask how many sessions until it runs, how many months of retainer you will actually pay, and which of the six factors above each quote excludes. Write the answers next to the figures from the same date, and the comparison stops being about which number is lower.

Because they could not be read from here, and the article says so in the method section rather than filling the gap with a number from memory.

## Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok: what actually differs between the closed models

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/closed-models-differences
Checked: 2026-11-19

What differs is not which model scores highest. Two leaderboards were reachable and are printed below with their settings, but neither is treated here as a quality ranking. What a buyer is stuck with is four documented things: the context window, the price per million tokens, whether tool calling and structured output are documented, and whether file and image input are supported.

## What does each vendor document?

Only what the vendor's own pages state. Where a page did not print a figure, the cell says "not captured" rather than a number.

| Model (vendor spelling) | Context window | Input / output, USD per million | Tool calling | Structured output | File and image input |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Fable 5.2 | 1M tokens | 8 / 40 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 1M tokens | 4 / 20 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| Claude Sonnet 5.5 | 1M tokens | 2 / 10 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | 1M tokens | 0.10 / 0.50, input qualified up to 100,000 tokens | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| GPT-6.2 Astra | 128K tokens short context | Short context 8 / 40, long context 16 / 60 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| GPT-6.2 Sol | 128K tokens short context | Short 2 / 10, long 4 / 15 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| gpt-6-luna | not captured | 0.10 / 0.50 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| deepseek-flash | 1M tokens | 0.15 / 0.60 off-peak, 0.30 / 1.20 peak | Documented | Documented | Vision yes, file not verified |
| deepseek-v4-pro | 1M tokens | 0.66 in off-peak, 1.98 out off-peak | Documented | Documented | Image not supported |
| gemini-4-neon | 1M tokens | 3.00 / 15.00 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| gemini-4-carbon | 1M tokens | 2.00 / 10.00 until 2026-11-30, then 4.00 / 20.00 | Documented | Documented | Image and file documented |
| grok-4.7 | 500k tokens | 2.00 / 6.00 under 200k context, 4.00 / 12.00 above | Documented | Documented | Image yes, file not documented |

The figures come from Anthropic's models overview, OpenAI's API pricing page, DeepSeek's pricing page, Google's AI Studio pricing page and xAI's models pricing page, all read on 19 November 2026.

Two cells need a note rather than a number. Haiku 5.5's input price is qualified on the page as applying to prompts up to 100,000 tokens. And GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol price short and long context separately, so both are printed. The capability cells are backed by the vendor documentation listed in Sources: PDF support for the Claude rows, file inputs for the GPT rows, and function calling for grok-4.7.

## What does a benchmark score not tell you?

Almost everything in the table above. The two leaderboards further down are printed with their settings, and neither is treated as a quality verdict.

SWE-bench serves its leaderboards through script rather than static text, and no dated snapshot was captured. The Aider polyglot page's visible top row carries a run directory dated 23 August 2025, which is not a snapshot of November 2026. Rather than cite either as current, this piece compares what you get and pay. A benchmark number also would not tell you the context window, the price, whether structured output is documented, or what the terms allow.

## What does one task cost at these rates?

Because input and output are priced separately, one worked example makes the table usable. The assumption is 100,000 input and 20,000 output tokens per task, and the rate is the printed price above.

1. Claude Haiku 5.5: 0.1 million input × USD 0.10 = USD 0.01, plus 0.02 million output × USD 0.50 = USD 0.01, so USD 0.02 per task.
2. Claude Fable 5.2: 0.1 million input × USD 8.00 = USD 0.80, plus 0.02 million output × USD 40.00 = USD 0.80, so USD 1.60 per task.
3. gemini-4-carbon at the price printed for Malaysia through 30 November 2026 (it doubles to USD 4.00 / 20.00 on 1 December): 0.1 million input × USD 2.00 = USD 0.20, plus 0.02 million output × USD 10.00 = USD 0.20, so USD 0.40 per task today and USD 0.80 after the change.

That is an 80 times spread between the cheapest and most expensive row on the same task, and every figure is checkable against the printed price. Change the assumption and the totals change proportionally; the multiplication is what makes it auditable.

![Three bars to scale: Claude Haiku 5.5 at USD 0.02, Gemini 4 Carbon at USD 0.40, Claude Fable 5.2 at USD 1.60 per task](/figures/closed-task-cost.svg)
*The same 100,000-in, 20,000-out task costs USD 0.02 on Haiku 5.5 and USD 1.60 on Fable 5.2.*

## Where is the lock-in?

Three places, and each shows up in the contract rather than the benchmark.

**Data retention.** Every closed model runs on the vendor's infrastructure. What happens to your prompts is governed by the terms, and the terms pages were listed but not opened for this piece, so I am not going to characterise them. Read yours before you paste a client's document.

**Model deprecation.** A closed model can be retired on the vendor's schedule. The prices and names above are dated for exactly that reason: they are a snapshot of a moving target.

**Export.** There is no weights file to take with you. Moving vendors means rebuilding prompts, tools and evaluation, which is a cost no table captures.

## Which vendor names drift?

The pages disagree with each other, and the table keeps the printed names rather than tidying them.

OpenAI's platform documentation sells GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, and prints the cheap model as gpt-6-luna, while its consumer page calls the family GPT-6. Gemini's marketing names differ from the API ids shown underneath them, which is why the table uses the API ids. If you are briefing a supplier, quote the API id, because that is what the documentation and billing use.

## What do the benchmarks actually say?

Two leaderboards, each readable only with its settings printed beside the number, and neither reconciling with the vendor names above.

SWE-bench Verified was read with the Bash Only setting and the mini-SWE-agent agent filter, sorted by percent resolved. Its top row is Claude 4.5 Opus (high) at 76.80% resolved for an average cost of USD 0.75 ([swebench.com, read 19 Nov 2026](https://www.swebench.com/)). The page states that its defaults are part of the figure, so a score quoted without those settings is not comparable to another SWE-bench number.

| Model (as the leaderboard prints it) | Percent resolved | Average cost, USD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude 4.5 Opus (high) | 76.80 | 0.75 |
| Gemini 3 Flash (high) | 75.80 | 0.36 |
| MiniMax M2.5 (high) | 75.80 | 0.07 |
| Claude 4.6 Opus | 75.60 | 0.55 |

Aider polyglot's visible top row is gpt-5 (high) at 88.0% pass rate for a total run cost of USD 29.08, but its run directory is dated 2025-08-23 and none of the visible rows is newer than August 2025 ([aider.chat, read 19 Nov 2026](https://aider.chat/docs/leaderboards/)). Those numbers cannot be presented as the state of the art in November 2026.

The names do not reconcile, and that is a finding rather than a formatting problem. The SWE-bench board prints "Claude 4.5 Opus", "Gemini 3 Flash" and "GPT 5.2", while the vendor table above lists Claude Opus 5.5, gemini-4-neon and gpt-6-luna. Different naming generations may not be the same models, so this article never claims that a vendor model in its table scores a leaderboard number.

## What did we not measure?

We did not run a benchmark ourselves. We read two, with their settings, and we are not treating either as a quality verdict: there is no "smarter" and no "better at coding" here.

Also absent by design: the Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek and Google terms pages were listed but not opened, so no claim is made about what they permit; gpt-6-luna's context window is "not captured"; grok-4.7's file input is not documented on the pages checked, deepseek-flash's file input is unverified, and Gemini's terms link was listed in the documentation nav but not opened.

## FAQ

### Can I compare these models by price alone?

Only if you know your token mix. Input and output are priced separately, long context costs more on OpenAI and xAI, and Haiku 5.5's input figure is qualified by prompt length. A model that looks cheapest per input token can cost more on a task that writes a lot.

### Why are some cells "not captured" instead of zero or a guess?

Because the page did not print the figure where it could be read. A zero would be wrong and a guess would be invented. "Not captured" is the truthful cell, and it tells you what to re-check on the vendor's page.

### Does Gemini belong in a comparison like this?

Only with a warning. Google sells it through a bundle that includes storage and other services, so its plan price is not line-for-line comparable with a bare chat plan. The API price above is comparable; the consumer bundle is not, and this article does not rank it.

## Do you need an API, or just a spreadsheet?

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/do-you-need-an-api-or-a-spreadsheet
Checked: 2026-11-19

A spreadsheet wins when the volume is small and one person owns the data. An API wins when two systems must stay in sync without a human copying between them. The deciding question is not the size of your business. It is whether a copy step still exists, and what it costs when that step goes wrong.

## What is the decision test?

There is one test, and it is a sentence you can say out loud: what happens in the hour after a change, and who has to move it.

Write down the last three changes to that data and how each one travelled. If every one needed a person to open two windows and retype, you have a manual sync. A spreadsheet is a perfectly good manual sync. An API is what you buy when the same retyping happens often enough to be a cost, or once too often to be tolerable.

## When does a spreadsheet win?

A spreadsheet is the correct tool in three situations, and buying an API in any of them is money thrown at a problem you do not have.

1. **The volume is low.** If the data changes a few times a day, the labour is minutes and the error is visible the same afternoon. Automating minutes is not worth a build, a key, and a monthly bill.
2. **One person owns the data.** Shared ownership is where spreadsheets fail, not low technology. A single careful owner with a sheet beats a half-built integration that nobody understands.
3. **The input needs judgement.** If a person has to look at a message and decide what it means, no API will do that part. Automating the transport while leaving the decision manual gains you nothing.

## When does it stop scaling?

Four signals, and any one of them is enough to start looking at an API.

1. **Two systems drift apart.** The sheet says one thing and the shop says another, and nobody can say which is right.
2. **The copy step has an owner, and that owner is a bottleneck.** When the sheet is only correct because one person is careful, you have built a dependency, not a system.
3. **A failure costs more than the fix.** A missed order, a double booking, an invoice sent twice. Once that happens monthly, the repair cost is real money.
4. **The data must move at night or at once.** A person cannot reconcile at 2am, and a batch of a hundred rows retyped by hand will contain errors you will not find.

## What does each one actually cost?

Not a like-for-like number, because no public benchmark exists for what Malaysian developers charge for this work, and we will not invent one.

What can be said honestly is the shape of the bill. A spreadsheet costs time, every week, forever, and it costs the cleanup after each mistake. An API costs a build once, a monthly fee for whatever it calls, and a maintenance event whenever a provider changes something. The build is the visible cost. The time you already spend, and the mistake that already happened, are the ones nobody puts in the sum until the sheet stops being enough.

## What is the middle option?

Plenty of Malaysian SMEs sit between the two, and it is worth naming the middle rather than pretending the choice is binary.

Exporting a CSV and importing it into the other tool is still a copy step, but a faster and more reliable one than retyping. A scheduled export with a fixed file layout, checked once a week by one person, can carry a business for years. It is not an API and it will not survive two-way sync, but it costs almost nothing and it fails visibly.

**Read next**

[What an API costs to wire up in Malaysia](https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-is-an-api-for-malaysian-sme)

[More on APIs and models](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/definitions)
## FAQ

### Can I start with a spreadsheet and add the API later?

Yes, and that is usually the right order. The sheet tells you which fields matter, which ones people actually change, and where the errors happen. An integration built before that knowledge exists tends to sync the wrong things very precisely.

### Is a spreadsheet insecure?

Not inherently. A spreadsheet that lives in a shared drive with access controls is a normal business tool. The risk is the same as any shared document: the wrong person gets a link, or the only copy sits on one laptop. Back it up and restrict the link; then the question becomes volume and drift, not security.

### What if my team already uses a tool that has an API?

Then the decision narrows to whether anyone has time to connect it. An API that nobody wires up is worth nothing, and a tool with no API that people use daily is worth more than a better tool sitting unused.

## Where your API key goes in a harness, and where it must never go

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/harness-api-keys
Checked: 2026-11-19

A harness keeps your key outside the conversation. It reads the key from an environment variable or from its own credential store at the moment it calls the provider. The key identifies your account, not each request, which is why it must never appear in a chat message, a committed file, a screenshot, or code that runs in a browser.

![A flow diagram: your app calls the harness, the harness reads the key from an environment variable or a secret store, sends it in an HTTPS request header, and the provider checks it against your account before the model answers. A second panel lists four places the key must never appear: a chat message, a committed file, a screenshot or log, and client-side code](/figures/harness-api-keys.svg)
*The key travels with the request but belongs to the account, and four places are permanently out of bounds.*

## Where does the key actually live?

In two places only: an environment variable that the process can read, or the harness's own credential store, which is a file on your machine.

Environment variables are the simplest form. In this harness a saved secret reaches the process as an environment variable named after the secret, and the harness reads it when it needs to call a provider. The credential store is the alternative, a file kept on disk rather than in your shell profile, which is why it can be backed up, permissions-restricted, and rotated in one place.

Either way, the key is a file or an environment, never a line in the conversation. That distinction is the whole article: the model never needs to see the key, and a harness that did put it in the prompt would be leaking it on every request.

## What does the key authenticate?

The account, not the request. The provider looks up the key, finds the account it belongs to, and applies that account's permissions and billing to whatever the request asks for.

Three consequences follow, and each one changes how you handle keys.

1. **One key is not one request.** A key used a thousand times is still one credential with one set of permissions. Revoking it breaks every caller that uses it, which is why you want separate keys per purpose rather than one key for everything.
2. **Spend limits belong to the account.** A leaked key spends your money at the provider's rate until you notice, not until the next request ends.
3. **The key does not say which tool asked.** The provider knows the account, not the script. So the audit trail starts with your own logs, not the provider's dashboard.

## Where must the key never go?

Four places, and they cover almost every real leak: a chat message, a committed file, a screenshot or log, and client-side code.

1. **A chat message.** Pasting a key into a conversation sends it to the model provider as part of the prompt, and the harness writes the conversation to disk. The key then lives in a transcript, possibly in backups, possibly in a ticket someone opens later.
2. **A committed file.** `.env` in a repository is the single most common leak. Even after deletion, the value sits in git history, and a public push is a permanent disclosure.
3. **A screenshot or a log.** Debug output that prints a whole request header, or a screenshot of a settings screen, carries the key without anyone intending it. Log redaction is a setting worth checking before you share output with a contractor.
4. **Client-side code.** Anything that reaches a browser is public. A key in front-end JavaScript, a mobile app, or a static page is available to anyone who opens developer tools, regardless of how it is obfuscated.

## What do I do when a key leaks?

Revoke first, then rotate, then investigate, in that order. Revoking is the only step that stops the spend.

1. **Revoke the key at the provider immediately.** Not delete the file, not change the password. Revoke the credential itself, because the file copy is not what the attacker uses.
2. **Issue a new key and update the one place it lives.** If it was in an environment variable, update the variable and restart the process. If it was in the credential store, replace it there.
3. **Check the provider's usage for the window between the leak and the revoke.** A key that was exposed for a week may have been used. The usage page, not the error log, tells you.
4. **Find out how it left.** Search your repository history, the transcript folder, and any shared documents. A leak with no identified cause will happen again.
5. **Narrow the new key.** If your provider supports scopes or spend limits, use them. A new key with the same broad permissions and no cap repeats the exposure.

The order matters more than the thoroughness. Teams that rotate first and revoke later usually keep paying for the same key.

**Read next**

[What an agent harness does with your request](https://upahje.my/en/articles/using-the-harness)

[More on buying and choosing tools](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/buying-guides)
## FAQ

### Should I use an environment variable or the harness credential store?

Use the credential store if you want one place to rotate and one set of file permissions to protect. Use an environment variable if the key is injected by a deployment system you already trust. Both are safe; a key written directly into a source file is neither.

### Can my team share one key?

You can, and you lose the ability to tell who did what. Separate keys per person or per integration make revocation surgical and make the provider's usage page readable. Sharing one key means any leak from any team member forces everyone to rotate.

### Do keys expire?

That depends on the provider, so check yours rather than assuming. A key with no expiry is a credential you must remember to rotate, and most teams do not. Set a calendar reminder if the provider offers no forced expiry.

### Sources

- DeepSeek Harness package metadata (credential storage behaviour observed on this machine) — https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh (checked 2026-11-19)

## Agent harnesses: who makes them, and what is actually open source

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/harness-landscape-open-closed
Checked: 2026-11-19

The four products a reader is likely to name are two different kinds of thing. Grok Bot from xAI and Dots from OpenAI are closed, hosted products you use through someone else's service. OpenBot and MausBot are source-available projects you can run yourself, and only MausBot's main repository is open source on its own licence. OpenBot is not.

## What is on the market?

One row per product, with the evidence level stated, because three of these were read from official sources and one was installed here and is now gone.

| Product | What it is | Licence or terms | Evidence level | Status | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenBot (nightly-labs) | Local-first desktop workspace for persistent AI teammates, with a plugin marketplace | PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0; repo licence field reads NOASSERTION | Official source, read 2026-11-19 | Active, pushed 2026-11-19, 9,037 stars | [github.com/nightly-labs/openbot](https://github.com/nightly-labs/openbot) |
| MausBot (OpenMausBot) | Open-source Grok Bot alternative with a virtual machine bots can use | Apache-2.0 on the main repo; a separate download repo carries MIT | Official source, read 2026-11-19 | Active, pushed 2026-11-18, 25,485 stars | [github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot) |
| Grok Bot (xAI) | Always-on agents with their own computer, working inside apps | Closed; signed macOS app, no public repo | Official source, announcement dated 2026-08-11 | Beta | [x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot](https://x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot) |
| Dots (OpenAI) | Always-on agents inside ChatGPT, with their own cloud computer | Closed; no public repo | Official source, announcement dated 2026-09-29 | Live, rolling out to Enterprise from 2026-11-18 | [openai.com/index/introducing-dots](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/) |
| DeepSeek Harness | Harness run by a profile, with MCP servers per profile | npm package, see package metadata | Ran here; no longer re-verifiable end to end | Installed 0.2.2-rc.1 on 2026-11-19 | [npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh) |
| OpenMausBot launcher (this machine) | A launcher whose payload is missing | Not applicable | Ran here; cannot run now | Orphaned | local, 2026-11-19 |
| Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode | CLI harnesses measured on this machine | Proprietary licences | Ran here, 2026-11-19 | Active | see [agent harnesses ranked](https://upahje.my/en/articles/agent-harnesses-ranked) |

## What do the licences actually let a business do?

This is the part worth reading twice, because "open source" and "source available" are not the same permission.

Apache-2.0, which covers MausBot's main repository, permits commercial use, modification and redistribution, provided you keep the notices. For a Malaysian SME that means you can run it in a business, change it, and put it in a product, without paying the project.

PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, which covers OpenBot, permits noncommercial use only. A business using it commercially needs a paid licence. That is the single most useful sentence in this article: OpenBot's code is readable and its site says "The source code of OpenBot is open", and its licence file says you may not use it commercially without paying. Read the licence, not the homepage.

Closed hosted products, Grok Bot and Dots, grant neither. You get access under terms of service, on the vendor's infrastructure, with the vendor's retention rules, and you cannot run them yourself or read the source.

![Three zones: closed and hosted for Dots and Grok Bot, source available for OpenBot under PolyForm Noncommercial, open source for MausBot under Apache-2.0](/figures/harness-licence-line.svg)
*Source available is not open source: OpenBot's licence is noncommercial, MausBot's main repo is Apache-2.0.*

## Why does one name map to several projects?

Because "OpenBot" is at least four unrelated projects, and the one installed on this machine cannot now be identified.

That is not a rhetorical caveat. `nightly-labs/openbot` is the desktop agent workspace in the table. Separately, `CopilotKit/OpenBot` is an MIT project with 12,887 stars described as an open alternative to closed AI bots, `ob-f/OpenBot` is a robotics project that puts smartphone brains in toy cars, and there are smaller projects under the same name. The directory that was installed here is gone, so which of them it was is unknowable now. A reader searching "OpenBot" today will find the robotics project first, and it has nothing to do with agent harnesses.

"GrokBot" has a milder version of the same problem: the GitHub repositories under that name are mostly community guides and clones about xAI's product, not independent harnesses. "Dots" also collides with an unrelated agent repository.

## What did we lose, and how do we know?

One harness that used to be installed here is now an orphan, and the failure message is the evidence.

The `openmausbot` launcher is still on this machine, and running it fails with a Node `Cannot find module` error naming a payload path that no longer exists. The payload is gone, there is no systemd unit under that name, and no data directory remains. So MausBot appears in the table from its repository, not from our use of it: we ran it earlier in this project and cannot now re-verify that experience.

## Which word should I use?

"Agent harness" if you want the vendor's own term, "harness" if you are talking to someone who already knows. "AI harness" is a modifier the vendors we read do not use. The vocabulary is covered in [agent harness, AI harness, agent framework](https://upahje.my/en/articles/agent-harness-vs-ai-harness).

[Agent harness, AI harness, agent framework: what the words mean](https://upahje.my/en/articles/agent-harness-vs-ai-harness)

[More on buying and choosing tools](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/buying-guides)

## FAQ

### Is OpenBot open source?

No, despite its site saying the source code is open. The repository's licence file is PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0, and GitHub's licence field reports NOASSERTION because it does not recognise a standard licence. Commercial use requires a paid licence.

### Is MausBot open source?

MausBot's main repository is Apache-2.0, which is open source and permits commercial use. Note the split: a second repository, `OpenMausBot/OpenMausBot`, carries MIT and describes itself as a download repo, so read which repository you are actually cloning.

### Does an open-source harness mean an open-source model?

No. The harness and the model are separate, and the split runs both ways: an open harness can call a closed model, and a closed harness can run an open-weight model. The licence you read applies to the harness code, not to the model it calls.

### Sources

- nightly-labs/openbot, repository metadata and licence file (PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0) — https://github.com/nightly-labs/openbot (checked 2026-11-19)
- OpenBot site (the claim that the source is open) — https://openbot.run/ (checked 2026-11-19)
- MausBot site — https://mausbot.com/ (checked 2026-11-19)
- milind-soni/OpenMausBot, repository metadata (Apache-2.0) — https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot (checked 2026-11-19)
- OpenMausBot/OpenMausBot, download repository (MIT) — https://github.com/OpenMausBot/OpenMausBot (checked 2026-11-19)
- xAI, introducing Grok Bot — https://x.ai/news/introducing-grok-bot (checked 2026-11-19)
- OpenAI, introducing Dots — https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/ (checked 2026-11-19)
- DeepSeek Harness package metadata, installed on this machine — https://www.npmjs.com/package/@deepseek-ai/dsh (checked 2026-11-19)

## How to brief an automation job so you don't pay twice

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/how-to-brief-an-automation-job
Checked: 2026-11-19

A brief that keeps you from paying twice names five things before anyone quotes: inputs, outputs, failure behaviour, the acceptance test, and who owns the credentials. A freelancer who quotes without those five is guessing. You then pay for the guess twice, once to build the wrong thing and once to repair it.

## What five things does a freelancer need before quoting?

Every one of these changes the price, which is why a quote that arrives without them is not a quote.

1. **Inputs.** Which system the data comes from, in what format, and whether you can give a sample of it. A sample file beats a description every time.
2. **Outputs.** Where the result goes and what it must look like on arrival. "Into my accounting software" is not an output; "a row in this sheet with these six columns" is.
3. **Failure behaviour.** What should happen when the source is down, the data is malformed, or a call times out. Retry, queue, or alert. Silence is a decision too, and an expensive one.
4. **The acceptance test.** The exact check that decides the job is done, agreed before work starts.
5. **Credentials and ownership.** Whose accounts the keys belong to, where they are stored, and what happens to them at the end.

## What does a brief look like?

Copy this, fill it in, and send the same document to every freelancer you ask. The point of sending one document is that you can compare quotes afterwards.

```
JOB: [one sentence, what should happen automatically]

INPUT
- Source: [system name]
- Access: [export file / API / manual upload]
- Sample: [attached file name, or "none available"]
- Volume: [rows per day, and peak]

OUTPUT
- Destination: [system or file]
- Shape: [columns or fields, exactly]
- Timing: [immediately / hourly / nightly]

FAILURE
- If source unavailable: [retry / queue / alert me]
- If a row is invalid: [skip and log / stop and alert]
- Who is alerted: [name, channel]

TEST
- Done when: [the check, on real data]
- Test data: [where it comes from]

ACCESS AND HANDOVER
- Keys belong to: [my account]
- Handover: [code, docs, a working test environment]
- Support after handover: [days, and what is covered]

BUDGET
- Fixed price required: yes
- Excluded: [anything you do not want included]
```

## What acceptance test should I agree up front?

One test, on real data, that either passes or fails without an argument.

The strongest version compares a known-correct result against the automated one. Take last week's completed orders, run them through the new automation, and require the totals to match the sheet a human produced. That test catches the failures that matter: a swapped column, a rounding difference, a status that never updates.

Agree the test before the work starts, in writing, and agree what happens if it fails. A brief with no test hands the definition of "finished" to whoever is being paid to finish it.

## What goes wrong when the brief is thin?

The same three things, in the same order, on almost every job.

The freelancer builds what is easiest to build rather than what you needed, because the brief left room. Then the price rises once the real inputs appear, because the quote was based on a guess. Then the handover leaves you with a working system and no way to change it, because ownership was never discussed.

None of that requires a dishonest freelancer. It requires a brief that could be read two ways, and two people reading it differently.

## How do I compare two quotes on the same brief?

Compare line by line against the brief, and treat an unanswered line as a gap rather than a bonus.

Ask each freelancer to price the same five sections and to mark anything excluded. Two quotes are only comparable when they cover the same work. A quote that is 40 percent cheaper usually excludes a section, and the section it excludes is usually failure handling.

Then ask both to walk you through the acceptance test. The one who can describe how it runs on your data has understood the job. The one who cannot has quoted a description.

**Read next**

[What automation work costs in Malaysia, from published rates](https://upahje.my/en/articles/automation-rates-malaysia-published)

[More on buying automation](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/buying-guides)
## FAQ

### Should I write the brief myself or let the freelancer propose one?

Write it yourself, even badly. A brief you wrote is the only document that states what you actually want, and it is the baseline every quote can be measured against. A freelancer's proposal is a price and an interpretation, and you want the interpretation to come second.

### What if I do not know the output format?

Get one real example first. Export the report or the row you want reproduced, and attach it. Most of the ambiguity in a brief disappears once there is a file that shows the target.

### Is a fixed price always better than hourly?

Not always, but for this kind of work it usually is, because the scope can be written down. Hourly suits work where the scope genuinely cannot be known in advance, such as investigating why a third-party service fails. If the brief is clear and the quote is still hourly only, ask what part is unknown.

## Open-weight models: Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral and Kimi, and what the licence lets you do

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/open-models-differences
Checked: 2026-11-19

The licence is the difference that decides whether you can use a model in a business at all. Of the five open-weight models read for this article, two are MIT, one carries a custom Qwen licence, one carries Mistral's own open-weight licence, and one carries a Kimi licence. "Open weight" tells you the files are downloadable; it does not tell you what you may do with them.

## What does each licence actually say?

The licence name and the restriction, quoted from the model card or its licence file, not from a summary.

| Model (vendor spelling) | Licence as published | What the card states | Parameters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 | MIT | "This repository and the model weights are licensed under the MIT License." | Not stated in card text |
| DeepSeek-V4-Pro-0813 | MIT | Same wording as above | Not stated in card text |
| Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B | Custom, `license_name: qwen3.8-max` | Licence text in the repo's LICENSE file | 2.4T total, 95B activated |
| Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B | Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License | Licence text in the repo's LICENSE file | 1 trillion |
| Kimi-K3.1-Pro | Kimi K3.1 Pro License | Licence text in the repo's LICENSE file | 2.8T total, 104B activated |

MIT is the permissive one: commercial use, modification and redistribution, with the notice kept. The other three are custom licences whose terms live in the repository's LICENSE file. Those files were not opened, so this article names the licences without summarising their terms. That is the honest limit: a custom licence is a document you read, not a label you assume.

## What does it take to run one?

Size is the first wall, and the hardware guidance on the cards does not give a minimum anyone can price against.

The cards state parameter counts of 95B activated within 2.4T for Qwen, 1T for Mistral Large 4, and 104B activated within 2.8T for Kimi. Mistral's card carries the only first-party hardware note among them: "`--tp-size 8`: example tensor-parallel size for a node of 8 GPUs", and it is an example rather than a stated minimum. The Qwen and DeepSeek cards point at vLLM recipes and the SGLang cookbook, which is community deployment guidance, not a first-party minimum. Kimi's card has a deployment section but the hardware figures were not captured.

So this article cannot tell you what self-hosting costs. A node of GPUs is a real bill, and no card here states the minimum configuration, so any figure would be invented. What it can tell you is what renting the same model costs.

## What does renting cost instead?

Every one of these models is also sold per token by its publisher, and the prices differ enough to matter.

| Model | Publisher's hosted price, USD per million | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| deepseek-flash | 0.15 in / 0.60 out off-peak; 0.30 in / 1.20 out peak | Off-peak and peak differ |
| deepseek-v4-pro | 0.66 in / 1.98 out off-peak; peak output 3.96 | Peak input not captured |
| qwen3.8-max | 1.50 in / 4.50 out | Card states this is the official version based on Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B |
| mistral-large-4 | 0.70 in / 2.10 out | First-party Mistral API |
| kimi-k3.1-pro | 2.00 in / 10.00 out | 1,048,576-token context |

A second host also sells DeepSeek V4.1 Flash: Mistral's API lists it at 0.30 in / 1.20 out, against DeepSeek's own off-peak 0.15 / 0.60. Same model card, two prices, which is the practical reason to shop the host rather than the model.

The arithmetic a buyer can do from here, at 1,000 input and 500 output tokens per task: deepseek-flash off-peak costs USD 0.00015 + USD 0.0003 = USD 0.00045 a task; kimi-k3.1-pro costs USD 0.002 + USD 0.005 = USD 0.007 a task. That is about 15 times the per-task cost, and both numbers are checkable against the table above.

## Which model should a Malaysian SME start with?

The cheapest per token that the licence plainly permits business use. On the rows read here, that is DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 at MIT, rented at 0.15 in / 0.60 out off-peak, before anyone buys a GPU.

That is a conditional recommendation, not a verdict: it assumes your task tolerates a Chinese vendor's API and that you do not need a custom licence review. If either condition fails, the next step is the Mistral or Qwen rows, both of which cost more per token and carry licences you must read.

## What could we not verify?

No card states a minimum hardware configuration, so no self-hosting cost is claimed. Kimi's hardware figures were not captured, and DeepSeek's peak input price is not published on the page read.

## FAQ

### Does open weight mean free to use commercially?

No. The licence decides that. MIT permits commercial use; a custom licence may restrict it, and you have to read the text in the repository's LICENSE file rather than trusting the words "open weight".

### Can I run one of these on a single GPU?

Not usefully for the models in this table. They run from 95B to 1T activated parameters, and Mistral's own example names a node of 8 GPUs. A single-GPU model would be a much smaller one, which this table does not cover.

### Is renting always worse than running it yourself?

No, and for most businesses renting wins because the node is expensive and idle most of the day. Running it yourself becomes a question when usage is high enough to beat the node's monthly cost, or when data location forces your hand. This article cannot price the node, so it does not pretend to draw that line.

- Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B model card and licence — https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B (checked 2026-11-19)
- Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B model card and licence — https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B (checked 2026-11-19)
- Kimi-K3.1-Pro model card and licence — https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro (checked 2026-11-19)

- Mistral AI, inference pricing — https://docs.mistral.ai/inference/pricing.md (checked 2026-11-19)

## Open or closed models: what a Malaysian SME can actually run in-house

URL: https://upahje.my/en/articles/open-vs-closed-models-malaysia
Checked: 2026-11-19

An open-weight model is one you can download and run on hardware you control. A closed model is one you can only call. For most Malaysian SMEs the practical answer is still closed, because running a model in-house needs a rented GPU, someone who can operate it, and a volume high enough to matter.

## What does "open-weight" actually let me do?

It means the model files are published, so you can put them on your own machine instead of calling the vendor's servers. As of 19 November 2026, Mistral's catalogue lists open-weight models under three licence shapes: Apache 2.0 for Mistral Small 4 and the Ministral 3 models, MIT for Z.ai GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, and a vendor-specific licence for Mistral Large 4 ([Mistral docs, checked 19 Nov 2026](https://docs.mistral.ai/models)).

Two things that fact does not give you: free inference, and permission to ignore the licence. Apache 2.0 is a permissive licence, but the terms are on the model page and they are what governs your use ([Mistral Small 4 page, checked 19 Nov 2026](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-small-4-0-26-03)).

## What does each option cost per month?

The per-call side can be computed exactly, because vendors publish rates. The self-hosted side depends on GPU rental, which we could verify for one supplier only.

| Cost line | Pay per call | Run it in-house |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you pay for | Tokens on each request | GPU time, billed by the hour |
| Verified rate | GPT-6 Luna: USD 0.10 per million input tokens, USD 0.50 per million output tokens. Mistral Small 4: USD 0.15 input, USD 0.60 output | DigitalOcean HGX B300: USD 7.94 per GPU hour |
| Monthly cost at 730 hours | Zero when nobody uses it | About USD 5,796 a month, before storage or a second GPU |
| Who runs it | The vendor | You, or whoever you hire |
| Who can change the model | The vendor, within their deprecation policy | You, when you update it |
| Where the data sits | The vendor's region | Wherever you rent the GPU |

The token rates are from OpenAI's pricing page and from Mistral's own model page, both checked on 19 November 2026 ([OpenAI pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), [Mistral Small 4](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-small-4-0-26-03)). The GPU rate is DigitalOcean's list price for an HGX B300, checked the same day ([DigitalOcean GPU pricing](https://www.digitalocean.com/pricing/gpu-droplets)).

## At what volume does self-hosting pay?

At a volume that no small business reaches: about 36 million messages a month, at the rates above.

The arithmetic, using a WhatsApp FAQ bot handling 3,000 messages a month at roughly 600 tokens in and 200 out per message:

1. That is 1.8 million input and 0.6 million output tokens a month.
2. On GPT-6 Luna that costs USD 0.48 a month. On Mistral Small 4 it costs USD 0.63.
3. One GPU at USD 7.94 an hour for 730 hours a month costs USD 5,796.20.
4. To spend USD 5,796 on GPT-6 Luna tokens you would need roughly 36 million messages a month, or 12,000 times the example workload.

Two honest limits on that number. The GPU price is one supplier's list rate for a high-end card, not the cheapest GPU time available, so the crossover can move lower. And a 119B-parameter model like Mistral Small 4 does not fit on one GPU at full precision, so the rate above is a reference for GPU time, not a capacity plan.

The comparison is also arithmetic, not capability. A model you run yourself is not automatically as capable as the closed one you were paying for, and that gap is the real reason most SMEs stay on per-call pricing.

## What does running one in-house actually require?

Five jobs, and none of them is a one-off setup.

1. Serving the model. Deploying an inference server, deciding on precision and batching, and keeping latency acceptable.
2. Watching it. GPU memory, error rates, and what happens when a request queues behind a long one.
3. Updating it. Open weights change; someone has to test whether a new version is better before switching.
4. Securing it. An endpoint that takes requests is an endpoint strangers can find.
5. Paying for idle time. GPU billing does not pause because nobody used the bot this afternoon.

This list is our description of the work, not a salary survey or a job specification.

## What should a Malaysian SME do this quarter?

Call an open-weight model before you try to run one. Mistral serves its own open-weight models through an API at USD 0.15 and USD 0.60 per million tokens, which gets you the licence and the model behaviour without buying a GPU or hiring anyone. Self-hosting becomes a question worth asking when your monthly token spend approaches a GPU's monthly cost, or when a data location requirement forces your hand.

**Read next**

[What an API costs to wire up in Malaysia](https://upahje.my/en/articles/what-is-an-api-for-malaysian-sme)

[More on APIs and models](https://upahje.my/en/articles/category/definitions)
## FAQ

### Do I have to run a model myself to use open weights?

No. Plenty of providers serve open-weight models through an API, priced per token. Mistral's own API prices Mistral Small 4 at USD 0.15 per million input tokens and USD 0.60 per million output tokens ([checked 19 Nov 2026](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-small-4-0-26-03)). You get the licence terms and the model without owning hardware.

### Can I run one of these on an office PC?

Not usefully. The models in this article are large: Mistral Small 4 has 119 billion parameters with 6.5 billion active ([Mistral, checked 19 Nov 2026](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/mistral-small-4-0-26-03)), and that needs a datacentre GPU, not a workstation. Small quantised models that do run on a laptop are a different trade, and this article does not measure their quality.

### Does self-hosting keep my data in Malaysia?

Only if the hardware is in Malaysia. Renting a GPU in another region moves the data there, same as calling a closed API. If data location is your reason to self-host, check where the rented machine actually sits before you commit.
